title: Dolphins Eavesdrop on Their Prey—and Each Other
author: Devin Reese
text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementZoologyDolphins Eavesdrop on Their Prey—and Each OtherThey strategically choose when to whistle or clickDRBy Devin Reese11:00 AM CDT on August 21, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleDolphins are a noisy bunch. They whistle to identify each other and interact socially. And their series of rapid-fire echolocating clicks allow them to feel their way around, acoustically checking out the contours of the underwater landscape and finding prey. These days, however, dolphins have to compete with a ton of different human-made noises, from oil drilling to ship traffic to explosives, that impair their communication. Subscribe to skip adsFeatured VideoPowered By 10 To Stay Alive, Some Bacteria Can Actually Shape-ShiftShareNextStayAdding to the acoustic melee, a paper recently published in PeerJ found that dolphins may be eavesdropping on fishes that make sound, such as drums (Sciaenidae) that croak by vibrating their swim bladders but are known to become quieter in the presence of dolphin sounds.Florida Atlantic University researchers with the Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute listened in on dolphins for two months along the Atlantic Coast from Fort Pierce to Jacksonville.
